Kevin Buzzard said:

I would strongly encourage the authors to jump through the #comparator hoop

I agree that comparator/formalization.yaml is a good idea. However, it seems to me that there is a need for a "comparator for dummies" exposition somewhere. When I posted something on this topic to MathOverflow yesterday and mentioned comparator, someone commented that they looked at the comparator GitHub page and couldn't understand what the point of it was. I'm sure that most mathematicians who are discovering for the first time how to vibe-verify something in Lean are going to have the same questions, and at the moment, there doesn't seem to be a good place to point them to. I don't think it's fully satisfactory to just give people instructions for what to do; there is a need for a beginner-friendly explanation of what exactly comparator does for you and why it is so strongly encouraged.

I think that if people are writing AI-generated code then all they have to do is to point their LLM at the comparator github page and say "please sort this out" (the LLMs they are using will necessarily be sufficiently smart to find this child's play).

Sure, but why should they do that? Because Kevin Buzzard says so? Actually, I think that's a pretty good reason. But I'm just saying that there is a need for a clear explanation of the purpose and benefit of jumping through this hoop. If people don't see the point, they're less likely to do it.

Also, a clear explanation will help illuminate what loopholes remain even with comparator. Otherwise, it becomes another black box that people trust unconditionally without understanding what it's doing.
If even OpenAI, with employees such as Boris Alexeev, did not bother with comparator, then doesn't that suggest that the case for it hasn't been made clearly and strongly enough yet?

If comparator really just takes a small number of tokens with any modern LLM, then that seems ideal, right? If the end user wants comparator, then they can use a few tokens and thus get the desired benefit?

I think that the community in general is trying to push the "comparator and formalization.yaml is the bare minimum to be considered a serious AI-authored project" idea so I was just pushing that idea.

Timothy Chow said:

Sure, but why should they do that?

Because comparator prevents cheating. Lean is a very flexible language, and a sufficiently clever AI can easily produce a lean file that appears to "prove the Riemann hypothesis" (for instance) in the sense that it constructs a term exactly like docs#RiemannHypothesis, and passes lake build with no errors/warnings. However, instead of actually having a proof, the file could instead:
(1) Use macros to redefine the meaning of identifiers in the theorem statement.
(2) Exploit runtime access to the computer's file system, altering Lean/Mathlib/Lake internals.
(3) Inject sorry via custom tactics, while disabling warn.sorry, etc.

I guess Timothy Chow's question (and also mine) is simply "What is comparator?"
If one open #comparator and start reading the readme, it just says "Comparator is a trustworthy judge for Lean proofs." and then a bunch of technical jargon. I still don't know what the Comparator does, why it is a trustworthy judge, why it can allow people to

Kevin Buzzard said:

immediately see what the claim is (and in particular whether the claim is what the authors claim it is), trusting only code in mathlib (which i trust) and I can also check that the formalization does indeed prove the claim without running random AI-generated code on my machine.

and why

Jack McCarthy said:

comparator prevents cheating.

My understanding is that comparator works perfectly if the statement can be written quickly only importing mathlb. One writes a file challenge.lean that only imports mathlib and a theorem

import Mathlib

theorem foo : RiemannHypothesis := by
  sorry

And a file solution.lean

import MyHugeProject

theorem foo : RiemannHypothesis :=
  riemann_in_my_project

What comparator does, if I understand correctly, is that the file solution.lean really proves what is stated in challenge.lean, without for example changing the definition of RiemannHypothesis (that in challenge.lean is taken from mathlib) or any other trick.

As far as I know nobody has ever tricked it (while it's very easy to trick #print axioms) so this is what the community consider the gold standard.

The obvious drawback is that if challenge.lean is 100K long because it contains a lot of definitions then it becomes very hard to manually check and, even if we trust comparator, we cannot be sure about what is saying.
Note that the code itself is very short (really really short, less than 1000 lines), so if one is interested they can check precisely what it does.

I can confirm both that:
1) AI can easily setup comparitor to run on github CI. It did it for me https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-claude/tree/main/comparator with no fuss.
2) it is somewhat of unusual setup, general OSS project in Rust or python doesn't have anything like this. Comparitor can only run on linux, which means local runs on macbooks don't work easily too. So a canonical page of extra motivation, that is separate from the technical documentation, would be nice.

python projects don't tend to come with the implicit claim that they can prove universal truths, for instance famous open conjectures (of course it doesn't stop people claiming their python code proves RH, but this is easily dismissed).

Not arguing that is not needed (it's a great tool and I think more projects should use it), just that unlike other general software practices - make sure the code builds, it is documented, dependencies are updated, etc., it is unusual.

Just in case the point I was trying to make gets lost: What I'd like to see is not just people talking about the benefits of comparator on this Zulip chat. I would like to see a well-written, beginner-friendly article or blog post that (1) explains what comparator is; (2) makes the case for its use; (3) points out the remaining (few) loopholes; and (4) briefly explains how to massage one's AI-generated Lean proof into an acceptable form. This article should be easily and publicly accessible, not requiring the reader to sign up for any kind of account, or dig deeply into some repo or archive.

Riccardo Brasca said:

As far as I know nobody has ever tricked it

Depending on what you mean by "tricked it", James Hanson has claimed to have tricked it at least once in the past.

I mean proving False. Anyway as any software it may have bugs (and the kernel may have bugs, the hardware may have bugs, a gamma burst can hit your CPU while it is performing a computation etc etc). The point is that this is our gold standard at the moment. #print axioms was the gold standard three years ago, it doesn't mean that it wasn't good, just that now we check against different things.

For anyone who might take on the challenge of writing such an article, I think it would be nice to explain, at a beginner level, some of the content of these threads: comparator and GMP, and SafeVerify passing kernel soundness exploit. On the topic of "gold standards," it might also be nice to briefy compare with Metamath Zero. (Incidentally, Mario Carneiro tells me that he recently got a grant to work on verifying the binary.)

Timothy Chow said:

Just in case the point I was trying to make gets lost: What I'd like to see is not just people talking about the benefits of comparator on this Zulip chat. I would like to see a well-written, beginner-friendly article or blog post that (1) explains what comparator is; (2) makes the case for its use; (3) points out the remaining (few) loopholes; and (4) briefly explains how to massage one's AI-generated Lean proof into an acceptable form. This article should be easily and publicly accessible, not requiring the reader to sign up for any kind of account, or dig deeply into some repo or archive.

I would ideally like to avoid spreading out information about comparator from its central documentation as it is still in slight movement every now and then. Could you describe what you are missing from the comparator README?

Regarding
(1) what comparator is: I will admit that the description at the header is a bit verbose, but that is intentional so we are very clear about the kind of guarantee we provide
(2) makes the case for its use: Would it be enough to explain the idea of verifying potentially adversarial Lean proofs or are you looking for something specific here?
(3) points out the remaining loop holes: these are pointed out in the correctness assumptions that I list at the top of the README. James' approach is an attack on assumption 4: "landrun works correctly on your system and Solution.lean does not exploit any bugs in landrun that allow a process to escape its sandbox" because he found a way to escape landrun which we subsequently patched
(4) briefly explains how to massage one's AI-generated Lean proof into an acceptable form, I would expect you can just dump the README into your favorite agent and it should get it.

In my view, the main reason that the README does not already provide what I'm looking for is that it already assumes too much knowledge of the reader. The first sentence is, "Comparator is a trustworthy judge for Lean proofs." The audience I'm imagining barely knows what Lean is, and doesn't understand why Lean itself isn't a trustworthy judge for Lean proofs.

Explaining the idea of verifying potentially adversarial Lean proofs isn't enough, I think. It would be good to give examples, whether real or hypothetical, explained in terms that a rank beginner can understand. The beginner has never heard of native_decide, for example. In what sense is GMP trusted? Is that something we should worry about? If it is, does comparator help? There was a Zulip thread a little while ago (can't find it right now) where someone ran some LLM trying to find Lean bugs and found some, but they weren't things that would get by comparator. Explaining some of those issues would also be of interest to a beginner.

Even a non-beginner may have some questions about what is gained from using comparator. It's not just the abstract concept of an adversarial proof that needs to be conveyed, but some concrete details of which kinds of adversarial behavior are being guarded against.

Another thing is that from Kevin Buzzard's point of view, it's not just comparator he wants to become standard, but also formalization.yaml. The README of comparator is not really the right place for a discussion of formalization.yaml.

I understand your reluctance to lose control of discussion of comparator. However, I also don't think that the README is the place to have this kind of extended discussion for beginners. That would clutter the README with a bunch of extraneous information. That said, there could be a separate file in the repo that fulfills the job I'm envisioning. It would have to be prominent, though; perhaps the second sentence of the README could point to this separate file.

One good location to put info about Comparator would be the "Did You Prove It?" page on leanprover-community.
I think formalization.yaml is a different discussion, maybe we need a new page like "Community Standards for AI Projects" or something.
btw cf. #AI authored projects > Can someone check my proof in universal algebra/clone theory @ 💬

Henrik Böving said:

I would ideally like to avoid spreading out information about comparator from its central documentation as it is still in slight movement every now and then. Could you describe what you are missing from the comparator README?

I think there should at least be an informal description of what it does and how it achieves it before it dives into technical jargon. The current readme looks like it is starting from the middle of a paper, skipping the introduction and assuming the reader has read three sections of hidden material.

At least something like: "The simplest configured comparator setup consists of a Challenge.lean, a file containing the statement that you completely trust, and a Solution.lean, a file that claims to prove the statement in Challenge.lean. The comparator then runs both of them in a sandbox and compares the two, to confirm that the statement proved in Solution.lean is indeed what Challenge.lean has specified" before the formal specification would be useful IMO.
This discussion has veered significantly off-topic. I suggest mods move this to #lean4 > comparator or a new thread.

(feel free to bikeshed the thread name, I believe @Timothy Chow can change it)
I changed the thread name to "Why should AI-authored projects use comparator?" Not necessarily the perfect thread name either, but good enough, I think.

This page from the language reference is probably also a good reference for what comparator conceptually is relative to other checks, and points out some remaining issues. However, I agree more examples of malicious inputs that each checker fails to catch would be more illustrating for people unfamiliar with Lean / checking proofs in Lean. https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs

Here's a first draft of how I would describe comparator to newcomers:

Comparator is a tool that prevents cheating in Lean proofs by separating the trusted and untrusted components of a Lean formalization into separate files. This blocks many well-known loopholes which would have otherwise allowed a malicious proof to make it look like a theorem has been proven when it actually hasn't.

A Lean formalization of a theorem consists of a Lean translation of the theorem statement, called the formal theorem statement, along with a Lean translation of the proof, called the formal proof. Lean's proof checker can verify that the formal proof is a valid proof of the formal theorem statement, but it cannot verify that the formal theorem statement is an accurate translation of the original theorem statement. For this reason, even if Lean verifies that a formal proof is correct, the formal theorem statement must still be proofread by a human.

The formal proof is often said to be untrusted because any mistake in it will be caught by Lean's proof checker, whereas the formal theorem statement is often said to be trusted, because Lean cannot detect mistakes in the formal theorem statement, and these mistakes can be catastrophic. However, due to the design of Lean, the separation between trusted and untrusted code is not always clear cut, and sometimes untrusted code can bleed into and change the meaning of trusted code. For example, a malicious user can submit a formal proof containing a line of code which looks like a helper lemma but actually redefines what addition means on the integers. In this way, a formal proof can tamper with the formal theorem statement (and in some cases, prevent Lean's proof checker from running in the first place) to make it look like something was proved when it actually was not.

Comparator is a tool that separates the trusted and untrusted components of a Lean formalization so that the untrusted formal proof cannot adversely affect the trusted formal statement. A normal Lean formalization consists of Lean files that mix trusted and untrusted code. In contrast, Comparator mandates that all the trusted code be placed in a file called Challenge.lean and that all untrusted code be placed in a separate file called Solution.lean. Comparator then runs Lean's proof checker in a special way that prevents anything in Solution.lean from cheating by tampering with anything in Challenge.lean or any other trusted component of Lean. When using Comparator, you are still trusting that Lean's proof checker is accurate and Comparator works properly, and you must still proofread the Challenge.lean, but you no longer need to worry about malicious proofs.

If you claim to have a Lean proof for a particular theorem and want to share it online, it is most convenient if you separate your proof into a Challenge.lean and Solution.lean that can be checked with Comparator. This saves time for people auditing your proof because they now only need to check Challenge.lean manually and no longer need to read your entire proof to ensure it does not cheat.

Niels Voss said:

The formal proof is often said to be untrusted because any mistake in it will be caught by Lean's proof checker, whereas the formal theorem statement is often said to be trusted, because Lean cannot detect mistakes in the formal theorem statement, and these mistakes can be catastrophic.

Although this is correct, the phrasing makes it sound like you got trusted and untrusted backwards

Perhaps there could be a clarifying remark that "trusted" means "unverifiable; you just have to trust it" while "untrusted" means "verifiable, so you don't have to just take it on trust." It is terrible terminology but it's probably too entrenched to change.
trustworthy / untrustworthy?
Though they don't really sound right to my ear

I personally would stick to verifiable / unverifiable. The word "trust" is just too confusing here. (Anyone else here dislike the saying, "Trust but verify"?) But, as I said, I think it's a lost cause. Are people really going to stop using the term "trusted kernel"?
In theory a kernel isn't inherently unverifiable thought, right? Isn't this part of the point of lean4lean?
Like "provability", "verifiability" is always relative to some assumptions. Something that is unprovable from one set of assumptions may be provable from some other set of assumptions.
